topics.name: Genetic drift
topics.kicker: Random shifts in a population’s alleles · Evolution by luck, not fitness
topics.dates: Happens in every population, but most in small ones
topics.briefing: Genetic drift is evolution by pure luck. In every generation, chance decides which individuals happen to pass on their genes, so some alleles (gene versions) become more common and others disappear, whether they help or not. It hits small populations hardest: after a typhoon in the late 1700s left about 20 survivors on the Pacific atoll of Pingelap, a rare kind of total color blindness became common there.
topics.answerHtml: Genetic drift (accept allelic drift or Sewall Wright effect; prompt on drift or evolution; do not accept “natural selection,” “gene flow,” “founder effect,” or “bottleneck effect”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1956, Peter Buri tracked an eye-color allele through more than 100 small populations of fruit flies, and over the generations many of those populations lost one version of the gene entirely. When this process pushes an allele’s frequency all the way to 100 percent, that allele is said to be fixed.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this mechanism of evolution in which allele frequencies change by random chance, especially in small populations.

tossups.p: Oliver Sacks visited Pingelap for his book _The Island of the Colorblind_. On that Pacific atoll, a typhoon in the late 1700s left only about 20 survivors, and because one survivor carried a rare allele, a form of total color blindness called achromatopsia [“ay-kroh-muh-TOP-see-uh”] later became common.
tossups.r: That disaster created a population bottleneck. For 10 points, name this random change in allele frequencies that is strongest in small populations.

tossups.p: Motoo Kimura’s neutral theory, proposed in 1968, says that most DNA changes that become fixed in a species got there through this process rather than through natural selection. Under that theory, much of the variety in DNA neither helps nor hurts survival.
tossups.r: This process can wipe out an allele purely by luck. For 10 points, name this random change in allele frequencies, strongest in small populations.

tossups.p: The Wright-Fisher model describes this process mathematically by treating each new generation as a random sample of the alleles in the one before it. In that model, every allele eventually ends up either fixed or lost unless new mutations appear.
tossups.r: Mutation, gene flow, and natural selection are the other main mechanisms of evolution besides this one. For 10 points, name this process in which chance changes allele frequencies.

tossups.p: After their numbers crashed, greater prairie chickens in Illinois lost many alleles and had fewer eggs hatch, until birds brought in from other states restored some of the lost variety. Biologists call a sudden population crash like that one a bottleneck.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this mechanism of evolution, strongest in small populations, in which allele frequencies change by luck rather than by natural selection.

tossups.p: Ellis–van Creveld syndrome, a rare inherited condition that causes short limbs and extra fingers, is unusually common among the Old Order Amish of Lancaster County, Pennsylvania, whose community grew from a small number of families. Ernst Mayr named the general idea behind cases like that one the “founder principle.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this mechanism of evolution, which includes the founder effect, in which allele frequencies change by chance.

tossups.p: The strength of this process depends on a number called the effective population size, which is often much smaller than a population’s actual head count. Because of this process, a new allele that neither helps nor hurts has a chance of spreading to the whole population equal to its starting frequency.
tossups.r: It can make an allele disappear by luck alone. For 10 points, name this random change in allele frequencies that matters most in small populations.

tossups.p: Cheetahs have remarkably little genetic variation, probably because their numbers crashed near the end of the last ice age, letting this process erase many of their alleles. In a crash like that, the survivors carry only a random sample of the original population’s alleles.
tossups.r: Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium assumes a population too large for this process to matter. For 10 points, name this mechanism of evolution in which chance changes allele frequencies.

tossups.p: American geneticist Sewall Wright argued that this process could help small, partly isolated groups cross from one peak to another on his “adaptive landscape,” as part of his “shifting balance” theory. One alternate name for this process honors Wright.
tossups.r: It works like sampling error in each new generation. For 10 points, name this random change in allele frequencies, strongest in small populations.

tossups.p: When a few birds blown to a remote island start a new population, they may carry only a small, unusual sample of the mainland population’s alleles, an example of the founder effect. A disaster that suddenly kills most of a population can have a similar result, called the bottleneck effect.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this mechanism of evolution in which allele frequencies change randomly from one generation to the next.

tossups.p: Without new mutations or migrants, this process steadily lowers a population’s heterozygosity [“het-er-oh-zye-GOSS-ih-tee”], the share of individuals carrying two different alleles of a gene. Because its effects are unpredictable, two isolated groups that start out alike will slowly grow apart genetically.
tossups.r: Unlike natural selection, it does not favor helpful alleles. For 10 points, name this mechanism of evolution in which allele frequencies change by chance.

tossups.p: Northern elephant seals were hunted almost to extinction by the 1890s, and although their numbers have bounced back, their DNA still shows very little variety. Because so few seals survived, this process had erased much of their genetic variation.
tossups.r: That crash is called a bottleneck. For 10 points, name this mechanism of evolution in which allele frequencies change by random chance.

tossups.p: By the early 1990s, only about 20 to 30 Florida panthers survived, and many had kinked tails and heart defects after this process stripped much of the genetic variety from their tiny population. In 1995, eight female pumas from Texas were released in Florida to restore some of it.
tossups.r: This process includes the founder effect. For 10 points, name this random change in allele frequencies that is strongest in small populations.

tossups.p: Tomoko Ohta’s “nearly neutral” theory argues that slightly harmful mutations can still spread by this process when selection against them is very weak. Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium can hold only if a population is so large that this process can be ignored.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this mechanism of evolution in which allele frequencies change by luck, not fitness.

tossups.p: Ronald Fisher argued that this process mattered much less than natural selection in large populations, a view that kept him arguing with Sewall Wright for decades. The founder effect and the bottleneck effect are two special cases of this process.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this mechanism of evolution in which allele frequencies change randomly from one generation to the next.

Unlike natural selection, it does not favor helpful traits: evolution by chance, not fitness

Bottleneck effect: a disaster or hunting crashes a population, and the few survivors carry a random sample of its alleles

Ronald Fisher thought it mattered far less than natural selection, a long-running argument with Sewall Wright
Described mathematically by the Wright-Fisher model, which treats each generation as a random sample of the alleles in the last
Motoo Kimura’s neutral theory (1968): most DNA changes that become fixed spread by chance; Tomoko Ohta added the “nearly neutral” theory
Pingelap: a typhoon in the late 1700s left about 20 survivors, and total color blindness (achromatopsia) became common; Oliver Sacks wrote about it in _The Island of the Colorblind_

Its strength depends on the effective population size, which is often much smaller than the actual head count
A new allele that neither helps nor hurts has a chance of spreading to everyone equal to its starting frequency
Without new mutations or migrants, it steadily lowers heterozygosity, the share of individuals with two different alleles of a gene
Ernst Mayr named the “founder principle,” the idea behind the founder effect
Founder effect: Ellis-van Creveld syndrome (short limbs, extra fingers) is unusually common among the Old Order Amish of Lancaster County, Pennsylvania
Greater prairie chickens in Illinois lost alleles after a population crash; birds brought from other states helped more eggs hatch
Only about 20 to 30 Florida panthers were left by the early 1990s, with little genetic variety; in 1995, eight female Texas pumas were released to restore it

trap.title: Chance or fitness?
trap.body: Genetic drift is one of the four main mechanisms of evolution, and tossups about it often mention the others, especially natural selection, so players blurt the wrong one. Drift changes allele frequencies by luck, while natural selection changes them because some traits help survival. The founder effect and the bottleneck effect are special cases of drift, but naming just one of them on a general question is wrong.
trap.fix: Chance, luck, sampling error, small or isolated populations, founders, disaster survivors, Sewall Wright, or Kimura’s neutral theory mean genetic drift. Adaptation, “survival of the fittest,” or peppered moths mean natural selection, and migration between populations means gene flow. Don’t mix it up with antigenic drift (flu viruses) or continental drift (geology).
trap.line: Real answer line: Genetic drift (accept allelic drift or Sewall Wright effect; prompt on drift or evolution; do not accept “natural selection,” “gene flow,” “founder effect,” or “bottleneck effect”)

topics.name: Stem cells
topics.kicker: Cells that can become many other kinds · How bodies grow, heal, and renew
topics.dates: First proved to exist in the early 1960s
topics.briefing: Stem cells are the body’s blank slates: unspecialized cells that can copy themselves and also turn into specialized cells, such as blood, muscle, or nerve cells. The ones in your bone marrow make billions of new blood cells every day, and flatworms called planarians use theirs to regrow a whole body from a small piece. In 2006, Shinya Yamanaka discovered how to turn ordinary mouse skin cells into stem cells, work that won him a Nobel Prize.
topics.answerHtml: Stem cells (accept stem cell or specific kinds, such as embryonic stem cells or induced pluripotent stem cells; prompt on pluripotent cells or undifferentiated cells)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In the early 1960s, James Till and Ernest McCulloch proved that these cells exist by injecting mice with donor cells and counting the lumps of new blood cells that grew in their spleens. The kind they found, called hematopoietic [“hee-muh-toh-poy-ET-ik”], makes every type of blood cell.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these unspecialized cells that can divide to copy themselves and can also turn into specialized cells.

tossups.p: Four genes nicknamed the Yamanaka factors, including Oct4 and Sox2, can switch an adult skin cell back into one of these cells. Shinya Yamanaka shared a 2012 Nobel Prize for creating those “induced pluripotent” cells, first from mice and then from humans.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these unspecialized cells that can develop into many different types of cells.

tossups.p: In 1962, John Gurdon grew tadpoles from frog eggs whose own nuclei had been replaced with nuclei from a tadpole’s intestinal cells, showing that specialized cells still carry every gene needed to build a body. Gurdon later shared a Nobel Prize with a scientist who turned adult cells back into these cells.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these unspecialized cells, which can be embryonic or adult, that can develop into many cell types.

tossups.p: E. Donnall Thomas won a 1990 Nobel Prize for developing transplants that give patients a new supply of the blood-forming kind of these cells. Donors for those transplants are usually matched to patients using proteins called HLA markers found on the surfaces of cells.
tossups.r: Bone marrow transplants replace these cells in patients with blood cancers such as leukemia. For 10 points, name these unspecialized cells that can become many kinds of cells.

tossups.p: In adult tissues, these cells live in niches, special neighborhoods of supporting cells and chemical signals that keep them from specializing too soon. When one of these cells divides asymmetrically, one daughter cell stays like its parent while the other goes on to become a different kind of cell.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these cells, found in embryos and in many adult tissues, that can turn into other kinds of cells.

tossups.p: In 1981, Martin Evans and Matthew Kaufman grew lines of these cells from mouse blastocysts, work that later helped Evans win a Nobel Prize. Seventeen years later, James Thomson’s team at the University of Wisconsin did the same with human blastocysts.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these unspecialized cells that can become many different kinds of body cells.

tossups.p: Hans Clevers’s lab grew tiny “mini-guts” called organoids from single cells of this kind taken from the intestine. In the small intestine, cells of this kind tucked into pits called crypts replace the organ’s inner lining every few days.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these unspecialized cells that divide to renew tissues and can become specialized cells.

tossups.p: Flatworms called planarians [“pluh-NAIR-ee-unz”] can regrow an entire body from a small piece because cells of this kind, called neoblasts, are spread throughout their bodies. Scientists hope to use cells of this kind to replace damaged tissues, a field called regenerative medicine.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these unspecialized cells that can divide and develop into many specialized cell types.

tossups.p: A zygote is described as totipotent because it can give rise to every kind of cell, including those of the placenta. Cells of this kind described as pluripotent can become any cell of the body itself, while multipotent ones can form only a few related cell types.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these unspecialized cells, which can be embryonic or adult, that turn into specialized cells such as blood or nerve cells.

tossups.p: The mesenchymal [“muh-ZENG-kuh-mul”] kind of these cells can turn into bone, cartilage, or fat cells. A ring of these cells at the limbus, the edge of the cornea, keeps renewing the clear outer layer of the eye.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these unspecialized cells that can copy themselves and develop into other kinds of cells.

tossups.p: Umbilical cord blood, which families can donate or store after a baby is born, is rich in the blood-forming kind of these cells. That hematopoietic kind lives mainly in red bone marrow, where it makes red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets.
tossups.r: Transplants of these cells treat blood cancers such as leukemia. For 10 points, name these unspecialized cells that can become many kinds of cells.

tossups.p: Cells of this kind make up the inner cell mass of a blastocyst, a hollow ball of cells that forms a few days after fertilization. Those cells are pluripotent, meaning they can become any type of cell in the body.
tossups.r: Adult tissues, like bone marrow, also contain cells of this kind. For 10 points, name these unspecialized cells that can turn into specialized cells.

tossups.p: A region of each hair follicle called the bulge holds a supply of these cells, which help regrow hair and repair the skin after a wound. Similar cells in the bottom layer of the epidermis keep replacing the dead skin cells that flake off the surface.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these unspecialized cells, found in embryos and adult tissues, that divide to renew the body.

tossups.p: Satellite cells, which lie along muscle fibers and wake up to repair them after an injury, are the muscle kind of these cells. Like many cells of this kind, they can form only a narrow range of cell types.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these unspecialized cells, which come in embryonic and adult types, that can develop into specialized cells.

tossups.p: In 2014, a team led by Masayo Takahashi in Japan performed the first transplant of eye tissue grown from reprogrammed cells of this kind, to treat a disease of the retina. Many plants keep growing their whole lives because regions called meristems hold a lasting supply of cells of this kind.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these unspecialized cells, which can be embryonic or adult, that can develop into specialized cells.

clues.t: Unspecialized cells that can divide again and again to make more of themselves (self-renewal)
Can differentiate, or specialize, into other cell types such as blood, muscle, or nerve cells

Bone marrow transplants give patients new blood-forming ones to treat blood cancers such as leukemia
Hematopoietic (blood-forming) ones in red bone marrow make red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets

Embryonic ones come from the inner cell mass of a blastocyst, a hollow ball of cells a few days old

John Gurdon (1962) grew tadpoles from frog eggs given nuclei from intestinal cells; he shared the 2012 Nobel with Yamanaka

trap.title: The cells, not the place
trap.body: Many clues describe where these cells live or come from, such as bone marrow, umbilical cord blood, a blastocyst, or a plant’s meristems, so players blurt the place instead of the cells. Others hear “totipotent” and answer “zygote,” or hear John Gurdon’s frogs and answer “cloning.” Words like pluripotent and multipotent only describe how many cell types these cells can make, so they earn a prompt at best.
trap.fix: If the question asks for “these cells” that can copy themselves and turn into other cell types, say “stem cells.” Specific kinds, like embryonic stem cells or induced pluripotent stem cells, are fine as long as the words “stem cells” are in your answer.
trap.line: Real answer line: Stem cells (accept stem cell or specific kinds, such as embryonic stem cells or induced pluripotent stem cells; prompt on pluripotent cells or undifferentiated cells)

topics.name: Hormones
topics.kicker: Chemical messengers carried by the blood · Signals of the endocrine system
topics.briefing: Hormones are chemical messengers: glands release them into the blood, and they travel through the body until they reach cells with the right receptors. Insulin from the pancreas lowers blood sugar, adrenaline from the adrenal glands gets you ready for “fight or flight,” and growth hormone from the pituitary helps you grow. Secretin, often called the first one discovered, was found in 1902, and in 1905 Ernest Starling named the whole group from a Greek word meaning “to set in motion.”
topics.answerHtml: Hormones (accept hormone; prompt on chemical messengers or signaling molecules; do not accept “neurotransmitters,” “pheromones,” or the name of a single hormone)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Ernest Starling introduced the name for these substances in a 1905 lecture, borrowing a Greek word meaning “to set in motion.” Three years earlier, Starling and William Bayliss had discovered secretin, often called the first one ever found, which tells the pancreas to release its juices.
tossups.r: Insulin and adrenaline are examples. For 10 points, name these chemical messengers that endocrine glands release into the blood.

tossups.p: Earl Sutherland won a Nobel Prize for showing that many of these substances do not need to enter their target cells, instead triggering a “second messenger” called cyclic AMP inside them. By contrast, the steroid kind of these substances, made from cholesterol, can slip right through the cell membrane.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these chemical messengers, such as insulin and estrogen, that glands release into the bloodstream.

tossups.p: Roger Guillemin and Andrew Schally shared a Nobel Prize for identifying the “releasing” substances of this kind that the hypothalamus sends to the pituitary through tiny portal blood vessels. The pituitary answers with more of these substances, which control other glands.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these chemical messengers of the endocrine system, such as cortisol and insulin.

tossups.p: Rosalyn Yalow won a Nobel Prize for the radioimmunoassay [“ray-dee-oh-im-yoo-noh-ASS-ay”], a method that measures the tiny amounts of these substances found in a person’s blood. Many of these substances are kept in balance by negative feedback, much like a thermostat turning a furnace on and off.
tossups.r: The field that studies them is endocrinology. For 10 points, name these chemical messengers, such as insulin, made by glands.

tossups.p: Charles Darwin and his son Francis showed that grass seedlings bend toward light only if their tips are uncovered, work that led to the discovery of auxin, one of these substances made by plants. Another plant one, ethylene, is a gas that makes fruit ripen.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these chemical messengers that, in animals, are released into the blood by endocrine glands.

tossups.p: Japanese scientists studying a fungus that made rice seedlings grow strangely tall, a disease called “foolish seedling,” discovered gibberellins [“jib-uh-REL-inz”], a group of these substances in plants. In insects, one of these substances called ecdysone [“EK-dih-sohn”] triggers molting.
tossups.r: In humans, these substances include insulin and adrenaline. For 10 points, name these chemical messengers made by glands.

tossups.p: One of these substances called calcitonin [“kal-sih-TOH-nin”], made by the thyroid, lowers the amount of calcium in the blood, while another one from the four small parathyroid glands raises it. The thyroid also makes thyroxine, one of these substances that contains iodine.
tossups.r: A lack of iodine can cause a swollen thyroid called a goiter. For 10 points, name these chemical messengers made by endocrine glands.

tossups.p: The posterior pituitary stores and releases two of these substances made in the hypothalamus: oxytocin and vasopressin [“vay-zoh-PRESS-in”], which tells the kidneys to save water. The pituitary, nicknamed the “master gland,” also makes several more that control other glands.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these chemical messengers, which travel through the blood to their target cells.

tossups.p: The kidneys make one of these substances, erythropoietin [“ih-RITH-roh-POY-ih-tin”], which tells bone marrow to build more red blood cells when oxygen runs low. The stomach and small intestine make others, such as gastrin, which signals the stomach to release acid.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these chemical messengers, such as insulin and cortisol, that travel in the blood.

tossups.p: When fatty food reaches the small intestine, cells in its lining release one of these substances, cholecystokinin [“koh-luh-sis-toh-KY-nin”], which tells the gallbladder to squeeze out bile. Unlike the digestive juices of exocrine glands, these substances are released straight into the blood, without ducts.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these chemical messengers made by the endocrine system, such as insulin.

tossups.p: Edward Kendall, who isolated thyroxine, shared a 1950 Nobel Prize for work on substances of this kind made by the adrenal cortex, such as cortisone. That outer layer of the adrenal glands also makes cortisol, the main “stress” one of these substances.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these chemical messengers, such as insulin and adrenaline, that glands release into the blood.

tossups.p: The pituitary releases one of these substances, somatotropin [“soh-muh-toh-TROH-pin”], which helps children grow, and much of it comes out during deep sleep. As evening gets dark, the pineal gland releases another of these substances, melatonin, which helps bring on sleep.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these chemical messengers made by endocrine glands and carried by the blood.

tossups.p: Each of these substances affects only target cells that carry a matching receptor, the way a key fits only certain locks. Compared with nerve signals, these substances act more slowly, but their effects usually last longer.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these chemical messengers, such as insulin, made by the glands of the endocrine system.

tossups.p: Oxytocin [“ok-sih-TOH-sin”], one of these substances, is a rare example controlled by positive feedback, since the contractions it causes during childbirth trigger the release of even more of it. Most of these substances are instead controlled by negative feedback, as when rising thyroxine makes the pituitary send out less of the signal that tells the thyroid to work.
tossups.r: Insulin and glucagon are two of them. For 10 points, name these chemical messengers released into the blood by endocrine glands.

tossups.p: Angiotensin II [“an-jee-oh-TEN-sin two”], one of these substances, raises blood pressure and also signals the adrenal glands to release another one, aldosterone [“al-DOSS-tuh-rohn”]. Aldosterone tells the kidneys to hold on to sodium, which helps the body keep water.
tossups.r: The adrenal glands also release adrenaline. For 10 points, name these chemical messengers carried by the blood.

trap.title: Messenger mix-ups
trap.body: Hormones, neurotransmitters, and pheromones are all chemical messengers, so clues about signals can pull players toward the wrong one. Hormones travel through the blood from endocrine glands; neurotransmitters cross the tiny gap between nerve cells; pheromones travel through the air or water to other animals. Many clues also name one example, like insulin or adrenaline, tempting players to answer that single substance instead of the whole group.
trap.fix: Blood, glands, target cells, the pituitary, or the endocrine system mean hormones. Synapses mean neurotransmitters, and signals between different animals, like an ant’s scent trail, mean pheromones. If the question says “these substances” or “these chemical messengers,” give the group name, not one example.
trap.line: Real answer line: Hormones (accept hormone; prompt on chemical messengers or signaling molecules; do not accept “neurotransmitters,” “pheromones,” or the name of a single hormone)

topics.name: Keratin
topics.kicker: Tough protein in hair, nails, and skin · Also builds horns, hooves, feathers
topics.dates: Named from the Greek word for “horn”
topics.briefing: Keratin is the tough, stringy protein that makes up your hair, your fingernails, and the outer layer of your skin. It also builds horns, hooves, claws, beaks, feathers, and even a rhinoceros’s horn, which has no bone inside. Its chains are linked by sulfur bridges between cysteine amino acids, which is why hair perms work by breaking and remaking those bonds.
topics.answerHtml: Keratin (accept keratins, alpha-keratin, or beta-keratin; prompt on intermediate filaments; do not accept “collagen” or “chitin”)

tossups.p: In the 1930s, William Astbury took X-ray photographs of wool and found that stretching the fibers changes this protein from an “alpha” form into a “beta” form. Mammals make mostly the alpha form, while birds and reptiles make a harder beta form.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this tough protein that makes up hair, fingernails, and the outer layer of skin.

tossups.p: This protein’s name comes from the same Greek word for “horn” that ends the name “rhinoceros,” and a rhinoceros’s horn is made almost entirely of it, with no bone inside. Cattle and goat horns instead have a bony core covered by a sheath of this protein.
tossups.r: It also forms hooves and claws. For 10 points, name this protein that makes up hair and fingernails.

tossups.p: The millions of tiny bristles called setae [“SEE-tee”] on a gecko’s toes, which let it cling to walls, are made of the hard “beta” form of this protein. Reptile scales and bird beaks contain that same harder form, while mammals make a softer, coiled “alpha” form.
tossups.r: Sheep’s wool is made of it too. For 10 points, name this protein found in hair, fingernails, horns, and feathers.

tossups.p: The pronghorn of North America sheds the outer sheaths of its horns every year, and those sheaths are made of this protein. Deer antlers, by contrast, are made of bone, not this protein.
tossups.r: This protein is rich in the sulfur-containing amino acid cysteine. For 10 points, name this protein that makes up hair, fingernails, and hooves.

tossups.p: Button-like junctions called desmosomes [“DEZ-muh-sohmz”] hold neighboring skin cells together by anchoring filaments of this protein inside them. Those filaments are a kind of intermediate filament, the middle-sized fibers of the cytoskeleton.
tossups.r: Skin cells fill with this protein as they die. For 10 points, name this fibrous protein that makes up hair and fingernails.

tossups.p: In a process called cornification, cells rising through the epidermis fill with this protein and die, forming the stratum corneum [“KOR-nee-um”]. The shell plates of hawksbill sea turtles, once carved into combs and jewelry called tortoiseshell, are also made of this protein.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this protein that makes up hair, nails, and the outer layer of skin.

tossups.p: Humpback and blue whales strain tiny animals out of seawater using comb-like plates of baleen [“buh-LEEN”], which are made of this protein. Whalers once sold baleen as “whalebone,” even though it contains no bone at all.
tossups.r: Rhinoceros horns are made of it too. For 10 points, name this tough protein found in hair, fingernails, and hooves.

tossups.p: This protein contains unusually large amounts of the sulfur-containing amino acid cysteine [“SIS-tuh-een”], whose disulfide bridges link its chains together. Perms work by breaking and re-forming those bridges while the strands are wrapped around curlers.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this protein that makes up hair, fingernails, and the outer layer of skin.

tossups.p: Colonial children learned the alphabet from hornbooks, wooden paddles whose lesson sheets were protected by a thin, clear layer of animal horn made of this protein. Softened horn was also pressed into combs, spoons, and see-through lantern windows.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this protein that also makes up hair, fingernails, and hooves.

tossups.p: A toucan’s huge but lightweight bill is a foam of bone covered by thin, overlapping tiles of this protein. The sharp, barbed quills of North American porcupines are also made of this protein.
tossups.r: Your fingernails are made of it too. For 10 points, name this protein that forms hooves, claws, horns, and hair.

tossups.p: Linus Pauling’s alpha helix, proposed in 1951, helped explain the X-ray pattern of the form of this protein found in mammals. Francis Crick then suggested that two or more of those helices wind around each other into a “coiled coil” in this protein’s fibers.
tossups.r: Horses’ hooves are made of it. For 10 points, name this protein that makes up hair, fingernails, and horns.

tossups.p: A narwhal’s long, spiral “horn” is really a tooth, so unlike a rhinoceros horn, it is not made of this protein. A rhino horn has no bone inside and is instead a packed mass of this protein’s fibers.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this fibrous protein that makes up hair, fingernails, and the horns of cattle.

tossups.p: When a snake sheds in a process called ecdysis [“EK-dih-sis”], the papery outer layer it leaves behind, including the clear caps that covered its eyes, is made mostly of this protein. Calluses on human hands are thick pads of dead skin cells packed with this protein.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this protein that makes up hair, fingernails, and the outer layer of skin.

tossups.p: Cats scratch posts and trees partly to pull off worn outer sheaths of their claws, which are made of this protein. The overlapping scales on a bird’s legs and feet are made of a hard form of this protein.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this protein that also forms hair, fingernails, horns, and hooves.

tossups.p: A bird’s beak is a bony core covered by a sheath called the rhamphotheca [“ram-foh-THEE-kuh”], which is made of this protein and keeps growing as its tip wears down. Pangolins, the only mammals covered in scales, have scales made of this protein.
tossups.r: It also forms feathers. For 10 points, name this protein found in hair, fingernails, horns, and hooves.

trap.title: Keratin or collagen?
trap.body: Keratin and collagen are both tough, fibrous structural proteins, so clues about strength and fibers can point either way. Collagen is the most abundant protein in the human body and fills tendons, ligaments, cartilage, bone, and the dermis, while keratin builds hair, nails, horns, feathers, and the outer layer of skin. Players also mix up keratin with chitin, the tough carbohydrate in insect and crab exoskeletons.
trap.fix: Hair, nails, horns, hooves, feathers, baleen, cysteine bridges, or perms mean keratin. Tendons, ligaments, a triple helix, or vitamin C mean collagen; insect exoskeletons or fungal cell walls mean chitin. Also check the noun: “this protein” is keratin, but “these cells” of the epidermis may want keratinocytes.
trap.line: Real answer line: Keratin (accept keratins, alpha-keratin, or beta-keratin; prompt on intermediate filaments; do not accept “collagen” or “chitin”)

topics.name: Leaves
topics.kicker: Plant organs that catch sunlight · Where most photosynthesis happens
topics.dates: Many change color in autumn as chlorophyll breaks down
topics.briefing: Leaves are a plant’s food factories: flat, green organs packed with chloroplasts that turn sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide into sugar. Tiny pores called stomata on their surfaces let gases in and out, and veins bring in water and carry sugar away. In autumn, many trees break down the green chlorophyll in their leaves, revealing yellow and orange pigments that were hidden there all summer.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: The arrangement of these structures on a stem, called phyllotaxis [“fil-uh-TAK-sis”], often forms spirals in which each new one sits about 137.5 degrees around the stem from the last, an angle linked to the Fibonacci numbers. Pairs of guard cells on these structures open and close tiny pores called stomata.
tossups.r: Their veins carry water and sugar. For 10 points, name these flat, green plant organs where most photosynthesis happens.

tossups.p: In the Namib Desert, _Welwitschia_ [“wel-WITCH-ee-uh”] grows only two of these structures during its entire life, and they keep lengthening from their bases for centuries, splitting into ribbons. A waxy layer called the cuticle helps these structures avoid drying out.
tossups.r: Most are attached to stems by stalks called petioles. For 10 points, name these plant organs that carry out most photosynthesis.

tossups.p: In corn and other C4 plants, these structures have Kranz anatomy, named for the German word for “wreath,” because a ring of bundle-sheath cells surrounds each vein. In most plants, these structures have a middle layer called the mesophyll [“MEZ-uh-fil”].
tossups.r: Stomata on their surfaces let carbon dioxide in. For 10 points, name these plant organs where most photosynthesis takes place.

tossups.p: As days grow shorter, many trees make red and purple pigments called anthocyanins [“an-thoh-SY-uh-ninz”] in these structures. A tree then seals off each of these structures with an abscission [“ab-SIZH-un”] layer at the base of its stalk so that it can drop off.
tossups.r: Their yellow and orange fall colors come from carotenoids that chlorophyll had hidden. For 10 points, name these plant organs that turn colors in autumn.

tossups.p: The bright red “petals” of a poinsettia [“poyn-SET-ee-uh”] are really bracts, colorful modified versions of these structures. Other modified versions of these structures include the spines of a cactus and the tendrils that pea plants use to climb.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these plant organs, usually flat and green, that are often attached to stems by stalks called petioles.

tossups.p: The sensitive plant, _Mimosa pudica_ [“mih-MOH-suh PYOO-dih-kuh”], folds up these structures within seconds of being touched, as water rushes out of cells at their bases. Venus flytraps catch insects with traps that are modified versions of these structures.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these plant organs whose stomata let carbon dioxide in for photosynthesis.

tossups.p: On cool, humid mornings, droplets of water can bead up along the edges of these structures after pushing out of pores called hydathodes [“HY-duh-thohdz”], a process called guttation. During the day, water evaporates from these structures in a process called transpiration.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these plant organs that are usually flat, green, and full of chloroplasts.

tossups.p: The crunchy stalks of celery are really the petioles [“PET-ee-ohlz”] of these structures, and rhubarb’s stalks are eaten too, even though the broad blades they hold contain poisonous oxalic acid. Tea is brewed from dried ones picked from a shrub called _Camellia sinensis_.
tossups.r: Their stomata let in carbon dioxide. For 10 points, name these plant organs where most photosynthesis happens.

tossups.p: The word “chlorophyll” combines a Greek word for “pale green” with the Greek word for these structures. Inside these structures, tall, tightly packed palisade cells lie above loosely packed spongy cells with air spaces between them.
tossups.r: Many of them turn yellow and orange in autumn. For 10 points, name these plant organs where most photosynthesis happens.

tossups.p: Silkworms feed on these structures from mulberry trees, monarch caterpillars eat those of milkweed plants, and koalas eat almost nothing but those of eucalyptus trees. Clover has compound ones, each divided into three smaller blades.
tossups.r: They are green because of chlorophyll. For 10 points, name these plant organs where most photosynthesis takes place.

tossups.p: The layers of an onion bulb are thick, fleshy versions of these structures that store food underground. Pitcher plants trap insects in deep, slippery tubes that are also modified versions of these structures.
tossups.r: Most photosynthesis happens in them. For 10 points, name these plant organs whose stomata let gases in and out.

tossups.p: In many plants, most of the stomata on these structures are on their lower surface, which helps cut down on water loss. Each stoma is opened and closed by a pair of bean-shaped guard cells.
tossups.r: Water evaporating from these organs pulls more water up through the xylem. For 10 points, name these plant organs where most photosynthesis happens.

tossups.p: Grasses, corn, and other monocots usually have long, narrow versions of these structures with parallel veins, while eudicots such as oaks and maples have branching, net-like veins in them. Each vein is a vascular bundle with xylem on its upper side and phloem below.
tossups.r: Most photosynthesis happens inside them. For 10 points, name these plant organs that are green because of chlorophyll.

tossups.p: Horse chestnut trees have palmately compound versions of these structures, with blades spreading from one point like fingers, while ash trees have pinnately compound ones, with blades lined up along a central stalk like a feather. Poison ivy has compound ones with three blades.
tossups.r: A red one from a maple tree appears on Canada’s flag. For 10 points, name these plant organs where most photosynthesis happens.

tossups.p: In 1779, Jan Ingenhousz [“IN-gun-howss”] showed that plants give off oxygen only in sunlight, and only from their green parts, mainly these structures. The giant Amazon water lily has floating, round ones that can grow more than 2 meters across.
tossups.r: Deciduous trees drop theirs each fall. For 10 points, name these plant organs where most photosynthesis takes place.

clues.t: Flat, green plant organs where most photosynthesis happens, turning sunlight into sugar
Green because their cells are packed with chloroplasts full of chlorophyll
In autumn, many trees break down their chlorophyll, revealing yellow and orange carotenoids
Deciduous trees drop all of theirs each year; evergreens keep theirs year-round
A red one from a maple tree is on the flag of Canada
Pores called stomata, opened and closed by pairs of guard cells, let carbon dioxide in and oxygen and water vapor out; in many plants, most are on the lower surface
Water evaporating from them (transpiration) pulls more water up through the xylem
Their middle layer, the mesophyll: tightly packed palisade cells on top, loosely packed spongy cells with air spaces below
A waxy cuticle on their outer surface helps keep them from drying out
Their veins are vascular bundles: xylem brings water in on the upper side, and phloem carries sugar out below
Monocots like grasses and corn have parallel veins; eudicots like oaks and maples have branching, net-like veins
Made of a flat blade and a stalk, called the petiole, that attaches it to the stem
Simple ones have a single blade; compound ones, like clover’s and poison ivy’s, are divided into several smaller blades
Cactus spines, pea tendrils, and the layers of an onion bulb are all modified versions
Silkworms eat mulberry ones, monarch caterpillars eat milkweed ones, and koalas eat eucalyptus ones
Their arrangement on a stem is called phyllotaxis; spirals often turn about 137.5 degrees (the golden angle) and follow Fibonacci numbers
_Welwitschia_ of the Namib Desert grows only two in its whole life; they keep growing from their bases for centuries
C4 plants like corn have Kranz (“wreath”) anatomy: a ring of bundle-sheath cells around each vein
In fall, many trees make red and purple anthocyanins in them, then seal each one off with an abscission layer at the base of its stalk
A poinsettia’s red “petals” are really bracts, a kind of modified one
The sensitive plant, _Mimosa pudica_, folds them up within seconds of being touched, as water rushes out of cells at their bases
The traps of Venus flytraps and the slippery tubes of pitcher plants are modified versions that catch insects
Guttation is the pushing of water droplets out of pores called hydathodes along their edges, often on humid mornings
Celery stalks are their petioles; rhubarb stalks are eaten but its blades hold poisonous oxalic acid; tea is brewed from dried ones
“Chlorophyll” joins Greek words for “pale green” and for this organ; the same root gives “phyllotaxis”
Horse chestnuts have palmately compound ones (blades spread like fingers); ash trees have pinnately compound ones (blades along a central stalk)
Jan Ingenhousz (1779) showed that plants give off oxygen only in sunlight and only from their green parts, mainly these organs
The giant Amazon water lily has floating, round ones that can grow more than 2 meters across

trap.title: Organ, not organelle
trap.body: Leaf tossups are full of photosynthesis clues, so players blurt the organelle (chloroplasts), the pigment (chlorophyll), the pores (stomata), or the process (photosynthesis) instead of the whole organ. Others answer “stems” for clues about modified leaves, like cactus spines, onion layers, or celery stalks, which don’t look like leaves at all.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun: “these organs” or “these structures” attached to stems by petioles means leaves. “This organelle” means chloroplasts, “these pores” means stomata, and “this pigment” means chlorophyll.
trap.line: Real answer line: Leaves (accept leaf or foliage; do not accept “chloroplasts” or “stomata”)

topics.name: Phloem
topics.kicker: Carries sugar from a plant’s leaves · Built from living sieve tubes
topics.briefing: Phloem is a plant’s food delivery system: living tubes that carry sugar made in the leaves to roots, fruits, flowers, and growing tips. Unlike xylem, which only moves water upward, phloem can carry its sugary sap up or down, wherever the plant needs food. Aphids tap into phloem to drink that sap, and peeling a ring of bark off a tree removes its phloem and can kill the tree by starving its roots.
topics.answerHtml: Phloem (prompt on vascular tissue or inner bark; do not accept “xylem”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Swiss botanist Carl Nägeli [“NAY-guh-lee”] named this tissue in 1858 from the Greek word for “bark,” and in trees it forms the inner bark. The vascular cambium adds new cells of this tissue toward the outside of a stem and new xylem toward the inside.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this vascular tissue that carries sugar from the leaves to the rest of a plant.

tossups.p: German botanist Ernst Münch proposed the pressure-flow hypothesis to explain how sap moves through this tissue. In that model, water drawn in by osmosis at a source, such as a leaf, builds up pressure that pushes the sap toward sinks.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this vascular tissue that carries sugar, unlike xylem, which carries water.

tossups.p: To collect pure samples of this tissue’s sap, scientists let an aphid feed, then cut its body away, leaving its needle-like stylet in place as a tiny tap. The sap in this tissue is under pressure, so it keeps flowing out of the cut stylet on its own.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this plant tissue that carries sugar both up and down, unlike xylem.

tossups.p: When this tissue is wounded, its sieve plates are quickly plugged by a carbohydrate called callose [“KAL-ohs”] and by a protein called P-protein, which keep sap from leaking out. Its sieve-tube elements are stacked end to end to form long tubes.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this living vascular tissue that carries sugar made in the leaves.

tossups.p: In conifers, this tissue carries sap through sieve cells, which are helped by neighbors called Strasburger [“SHTRAHS-boor-ger”] cells or albuminous cells. Flowering plants instead use sieve-tube elements, each supported by a companion cell.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this vascular tissue that carries sugar from leaves to the rest of the plant.

tossups.p: Mature sieve-tube elements in this tissue have no nucleus, so they depend on companion cells, which are linked to them by many tiny channels called plasmodesmata [“plaz-muh-dez-MAH-tuh”]. Each sieve-tube element is joined to the next by a perforated end wall called a sieve plate.
tossups.r: Companion cells also load sucrose into it. For 10 points, name this vascular tissue that carries food made in the leaves.

tossups.p: Linen cloth is woven from the long, tough bast fibers of flax plants, which come from this tissue, and jute rope is made from similar fibers. In a tree, this tissue lies under the corky outer bark, forming the inner bark.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this vascular tissue that carries sugar, unlike the water-carrying xylem.

tossups.p: Citrus greening, a disease that has hurt orange groves in Florida, is caused by a bacterium that lives in this tissue and is spread by tiny insects called psyllids [“SIL-idz”]. Many plant viruses also spread through a plant by riding along in this tissue’s sap.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this living plant tissue that carries sugar both up and down.

tossups.p: Larvae of the emerald ash borer, an invasive beetle, kill ash trees by tunneling through this tissue and the cambium just under the bark. Girdling a tree, by cutting away a complete ring of bark, destroys this tissue all the way around the trunk.
tossups.r: The tree’s roots then starve. For 10 points, name this vascular tissue that carries sugar from the leaves.

tossups.p: The flowering signal called florigen, which turned out to be a protein named FT, travels from the leaves to the tips of shoots through this tissue. In leaf veins, this tissue usually lies on the lower side, below the xylem.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this vascular tissue that carries sugar, made of sieve tubes and companion cells.

tossups.p: Movement through this tissue, called translocation, carries sap from sources, such as mature leaves, to sinks, such as roots, fruits, and growing tips. A growing potato tuber is a sink that stores what it receives as starch.
tossups.r: Its sap can flow up or down. For 10 points, name this vascular tissue that carries sugar.

tossups.p: In many roots, strands of this tissue sit between the arms of an X-shaped core of xylem. In a typical stem, this tissue sits on the outer side of each vascular bundle, with xylem on the inner side.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this living vascular tissue that carries sugar from the leaves to the rest of a plant.

tossups.p: Some ants guard aphids like herds of cattle and stroke them to collect honeydew, a sticky waste the aphids make from this tissue’s sap. Mosses and liverworts lack both this tissue and xylem, which helps keep them small.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this tissue that carries sugar made in the leaves, unlike xylem, which carries water.

tossups.p: Cinnamon sticks are curls of the dried inner bark of certain tropical trees, a layer made mostly of this tissue. In a tree trunk, only a thin layer of this tissue next to the vascular cambium still carries sap; older layers are crushed outward into the bark.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this vascular tissue that carries sugar both up and down a plant.

tossups.p: Companion cells are packed with mitochondria, since they spend ATP pumping sucrose into this tissue, a step called loading. Unloading at the other end lets fruits, seeds, and roots store what this tissue brings them.
tossups.r: Sugar beets and sugarcane store huge amounts of the sucrose it delivers. For 10 points, name this vascular tissue that carries sugar from the leaves.

clues.t: Plant tissue that carries sugar (food) made in the leaves to the rest of the plant
One of the two vascular tissues, along with xylem, which carries water; mosses lack both
Its sap can flow up and down, while water in xylem moves only upward
Its conducting cells are alive when they work, unlike the dead, hollow cells of xylem
Sap flows through sieve-tube elements stacked end to end and joined by perforated walls called sieve plates
Mature sieve-tube elements have no nucleus, so neighboring companion cells keep them running
Moving sap through it is called translocation
Sap moves from sources, like mature leaves, to sinks, like roots, fruits, growing tips, and potato tubers
Carries sugar mainly as sucrose dissolved in water; sugar beets and sugarcane store huge amounts of it
Aphids drink its sap and release sticky honeydew, which some ants collect by guarding aphids like cattle
In trees it forms the inner bark; the vascular cambium adds it toward the outside and xylem toward the inside
Lies on the outer side of each vascular bundle in a stem, and on the lower side of leaf veins, below the xylem
Girdling, cutting away a ring of bark, destroys it all the way around and can kill a tree by starving its roots
Swiss botanist Carl Nägeli named it in 1858, from the Greek word for “bark”
Ernst Münch’s pressure-flow hypothesis: water drawn in by osmosis at a source builds pressure that pushes sap toward sinks
When it is wounded, sieve plates are plugged by a carbohydrate called callose and by P-protein
Scientists sample its sap by cutting away a feeding aphid and leaving its stylet in place; the sap flows out under pressure
Companion cells connect to sieve-tube elements through many tiny channels called plasmodesmata
Conifers use sieve cells helped by Strasburger (albuminous) cells instead of sieve tubes and companion cells
Its tough bast fibers give linen (from flax) and jute rope
Citrus greening, spread by tiny insects called psyllids, comes from a bacterium living in it; many plant viruses travel in its sap
Emerald ash borer larvae kill ash trees by tunneling through it and the cambium just under the bark
The flowering signal florigen, a protein named FT, travels through it from the leaves to the shoot tips
Companion cells, packed with mitochondria, spend ATP pumping sucrose into it, a step called loading
Cinnamon is the dried inner bark of certain trees, a layer made mostly of it; only its thin newest layer still carries sap
In many roots, its strands sit between the arms of an X-shaped core of xylem

trap.title: Phloem or xylem?
trap.body: Phloem and xylem are the two vascular tissues, and tossups often mention both. Phloem carries sugar from the leaves, in either direction, through living sieve-tube cells; xylem carries water and minerals up from the roots through dead, hollow cells. The vascular cambium, which makes new phloem and xylem, is a third answer players confuse with both.
trap.fix: Sugar, sucrose, sources and sinks, sieve tubes, companion cells, aphids, girdling, or the inner bark mean phloem. Water, minerals, transpiration, tracheids, vessel elements, wood, tree rings, or maple sap mean xylem. A memory trick: phloem carries food.
trap.line: Real answer line: Phloem (prompt on vascular tissue or inner bark; do not accept “xylem”)

topics.name: Lipids
topics.kicker: Fats, oils, waxes, and steroids · Store energy and build cell membranes
topics.briefing: Lipids are the greasy, water-fearing molecules of life: fats, oils, waxes, and steroids such as cholesterol. Because they are nonpolar, they don’t dissolve in water, which is why oil-and-vinegar salad dressing separates. Fats pack about 9 Calories per gram, more than twice as much as carbohydrates or proteins, and phospholipids form the double layer that wraps every cell.
topics.answerHtml: Lipids (accept fats or lipid; prompt on triglycerides or oils; do not accept “fatty acids” or “carbohydrates”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In the early 1800s, French chemist Michel Chevreul [“shuh-VRUHL”] showed that soap-making splits animal versions of these substances into glycerol and acids. That reaction, in which these substances are boiled with lye, is called saponification [“suh-pon-ih-fih-KAY-shun”].
tossups.r: They store about 9 Calories per gram. For 10 points, name this class of water-fearing biomolecules that includes oils, waxes, and steroids.

tossups.p: Omega-3 molecules of this kind, found in fish such as salmon, have their first carbon-carbon double bond three carbons from the tail end of the chain. Linoleic [“lin-uh-LEE-ik”] acid, another one, is called “essential” because the body cannot make it and must get it from food.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this class of biomolecules that includes triglycerides and steroids and does not dissolve in water.

tossups.p: Lecithin [“LESS-ih-thin”] from egg yolks keeps mayonnaise from separating, since each of its molecules has a water-loving head and two water-fearing tails. Molecules with that shape, one type of these substances, are called amphipathic [“am-fih-PATH-ik”].
tossups.r: That type forms the double layer of every cell membrane. For 10 points, name this class of biomolecules that also includes oils and waxes.

tossups.p: Bubbling hydrogen gas through liquid plant-based examples of these substances turns some of their carbon-carbon double bonds into single bonds, making solid spreads like margarine. That partial hydrogenation also creates “trans” versions of these molecules, which are linked to heart disease.
tossups.r: Saturated ones, like butter, have no double bonds and are solid at room temperature. For 10 points, name these biomolecules that include triglycerides.

tossups.p: In the emulsion test for these substances, a food sample is shaken with ethanol and then poured into water, where these substances turn the mixture cloudy white. The dye Sudan III [“soo-DAN three”] stains these substances red.
tossups.r: Rubbing them on brown paper leaves a see-through spot. For 10 points, name these biomolecules that include oils and waxes.

tossups.p: After digestion, these molecules are packed into particles called chylomicrons [“kye-loh-MY-kronz”] and absorbed into lacteals, tiny lymph vessels inside the villi of the small intestine. Before that, bile salts help gather them into tiny clusters called micelles [“my-SELZ”].
tossups.r: Enzymes called lipases break them down. For 10 points, name these energy-rich biomolecules that do not dissolve in water.

tossups.p: Brown adipose tissue burns stored molecules of this kind to make heat instead of ATP, using a protein called thermogenin inside its mitochondria. White adipose tissue stores these molecules and also cushions organs and insulates the body.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these biomolecules, including triglycerides, that store about 9 Calories of energy per gram.

tossups.p: Three ester bonds form when a glycerol molecule joins three long acid chains in a dehydration synthesis that releases three molecules of water. The molecule built that way, a triglyceride [“try-GLISS-er-ide”], is the most common kind of these substances in food.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this class of biomolecules that includes oils, waxes, and steroids such as cholesterol.

tossups.p: The myelin sheaths that insulate nerve fibers are made mostly of these substances, which is one reason the brain is so rich in them. One group of these substances, which includes testosterone and estrogen, is built from four fused carbon rings.
tossups.r: That group, the steroids, includes cholesterol. For 10 points, name this class of water-fearing biomolecules.

tossups.p: Cells that make large amounts of these substances, such as those in the adrenal glands, are packed with smooth endoplasmic reticulum, the organelle that builds them. Vitamins A, D, E, and K dissolve in these substances rather than in water, so the body can store them.
tossups.r: They do not mix with water. For 10 points, name this class of biomolecules that includes oils, waxes, and cholesterol.

tossups.p: When food rich in these substances reaches the small intestine, the gut releases cholecystokinin [“koh-luh-sis-toh-KY-nin”], which makes the gallbladder squeeze out bile. Bile then breaks these substances into tiny droplets so enzymes can reach them, a process called emulsification.
tossups.r: Pancreatic lipase then breaks them into fatty acids and glycerol. For 10 points, name these biomolecules that do not dissolve in water.

tossups.p: Chips and nuts go rancid when oxygen attacks the double bonds in these molecules, so companies add antioxidants such as vitamin E to slow the damage. Unsaturated versions of these molecules have kinks at those double bonds, which keep them liquid at room temperature.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this class of biomolecules, including oils and waxes, that stores long-term energy.

tossups.p: A camel’s hump is not a water tank but a store of these substances, which the camel can break down for energy when food is scarce. Whales and seals stay warm in icy water thanks to blubber, a thick layer of these substances under the skin.
tossups.r: Butter and olive oil are rich in them. For 10 points, name this class of biomolecules that includes triglycerides, oils, and waxes.

tossups.p: Soap cleans greasy dishes because each soap molecule has a long nonpolar tail that dissolves in these substances and a charged head that dissolves in water. Bile salts work in a similar way, coating tiny droplets of these substances in the small intestine.
tossups.r: These substances are nonpolar, so they don’t mix with water. For 10 points, name this class of biomolecules.

tossups.p: Fish that live in icy water build their cell membranes with extra unsaturated molecules of this kind, whose kinked tails keep the membranes from stiffening in the cold. Saturated molecules of this kind have straight tails that pack tightly together.
tossups.r: That is why butter is solid at room temperature. For 10 points, name this class of biomolecules that includes oils and waxes.

Enzymes called lipases, mostly from the pancreas, break them into fatty acids and glycerol

Boiling them with lye, a strong base, makes soap and glycerol, a reaction called saponification

Bile salts gather them into micelles; then they are packed into chylomicrons and absorbed by lacteals in the villi
Lecithin from egg yolks keeps mayonnaise from separating; its molecules are amphipathic, with a water-loving head and two water-fearing tails

trap.title: The family, not one member
trap.body: Lipid tossups name many family members, such as triglycerides, phospholipids, cholesterol, and waxes, and many parts, such as fatty acids and glycerol, so players blurt one of those instead of the whole class. “Triglycerides” or “oils” earns only a prompt, and “fatty acids” is wrong because fatty acids are just building blocks. Players also confuse lipids with carbohydrates, since both store energy and are made mostly of carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen.
trap.fix: If the question asks for the whole class, including steroids, waxes, or membrane molecules, say “lipids” (or “fats”). Water-fearing, nonpolar, 9 Calories per gram, Sudan III, or bile mean lipids; sugars, starch, 4 Calories per gram, or Benedict’s and iodine tests mean carbohydrates.
trap.line: Real answer line: Lipids (accept fats or lipid; prompt on triglycerides or oils; do not accept “fatty acids” or “carbohydrates”)

topics.name: Marsupials
topics.kicker: Pouched mammals like kangaroos and koalas · Most live in Australia
topics.dates: The Virginia opossum is the only one north of Mexico
topics.briefing: Marsupials are mammals that give birth to tiny, underdeveloped babies, which usually keep growing inside the mother’s pouch. A newborn red kangaroo is about the size of a jellybean, yet it crawls into the pouch on its own and stays there for months as a “joey.” Most marsupials, including kangaroos, koalas, wombats, and Tasmanian devils, live in Australia and New Guinea, but opossums live in the Americas.
topics.answerHtml: Marsupials (accept Marsupialia, metatherians, or pouched mammals; prompt on mammals; do not accept “monotremes” or “placental mammals”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: The largest member of this group ever, _Diprotodon_ [“dye-PROH-tuh-don”], was a rhinoceros-sized plant-eater that died out tens of thousands of years ago. Fossils show that members of this group once lived in Antarctica, which linked South America to Australia.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this group of mammals, including kangaroos and koalas, whose young usually grow in a pouch.

tossups.p: In 1770, members of James Cook’s expedition wrote down the Guugu Yimithirr [“GOO-goo YIM-ih-theer”] word gangurru, which became the English name for some of these animals. Members of this group called macropods, a name meaning “big foot,” hop on long hind feet.
tossups.r: Those animals are kangaroos. For 10 points, name this group of mammals whose babies, called joeys, usually grow in a pouch.

tossups.p: An island near Perth got the name Rottnest, meaning “rat’s nest,” after a Dutch explorer mistook its quokkas [“KWOK-uhz”], small members of this group, for giant rats. The numbat, another member of this group, eats almost nothing but termites.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this group of mammals, including kangaroos, koalas, and wombats, that usually carry their young in a pouch.

tossups.p: The monito del monte [“moh-NEE-toh del MON-tay”], a tiny member of this group from the forests of Chile and Argentina, is more closely related to members on another continent than to the opossums living around it. Shrew opossums form another South American branch of this group.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this group of mammals, including kangaroos and koalas, whose young usually grow in a pouch.

tossups.p: The last known thylacine [“THY-luh-seen”], a striped, dog-like meat-eater of this group nicknamed the Tasmanian tiger, died in a zoo in Hobart in 1936. Because thylacines looked so much like wolves without being closely related, they are a classic example of convergent evolution.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this group of mammals, including the Tasmanian devil and the koala, that usually raise their young in a pouch.

tossups.p: One member of this group has fingerprints so similar to human ones that they can be hard to tell apart under a microscope. That animal eats almost nothing but eucalyptus leaves and sleeps up to about 20 hours a day.
tossups.r: That animal is the koala, which is not a bear. For 10 points, name this group of mammals whose young usually grow in a pouch.

tossups.p: At Easter, some stores sell chocolate bilbies instead of bunnies to help protect the bilby, a big-eared, burrowing member of this group. The sugar glider, another member of this group, glides between trees on flaps of skin stretched between its front and back legs.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this group of mammals, including wombats and kangaroos, whose young usually grow in a pouch.

tossups.p: The only member of this group native to the United States and Canada has 50 teeth, a prehensile tail, and thumb-like big toes on its hind feet. When threatened, that animal may “play possum,” going limp and pretending to be dead.
tossups.r: That animal is the Virginia opossum. For 10 points, name this group of mammals whose young usually grow in a pouch.

tossups.p: Wild populations of the largest living meat-eating member of this group have shrunk because of devil facial tumor disease, a contagious cancer that spreads between animals when they bite each other. The Looney Tunes cartoon character Taz is based on that animal.
tossups.r: That animal is the Tasmanian devil. For 10 points, name this group of mammals, including kangaroos and koalas, whose newborns crawl into a pouch.

tossups.p: When grazing slowly, the biggest living members of this group lean on their thick, muscular tails as a fifth leg, a gait called pentapedal [“pen-tuh-PEE-dul”] locomotion. At higher speeds, springy tendons in their long hind legs store energy with each hop.
tossups.r: Those animals are red kangaroos. For 10 points, name this group of mammals whose babies are called joeys.

tossups.p: One burrowing member of this group leaves cube-shaped droppings, which it piles on rocks and logs to mark its territory, and scientists who studied how it makes those cubes won a 2019 Ig Nobel Prize. Its teeth never stop growing, much like a rodent’s front teeth.
tossups.r: That animal is the wombat, whose pouch faces backward. For 10 points, name this group of mammals, including kangaroos.

tossups.p: Crash, the hero of a video game series that began in 1996, is a bandicoot, a long-snouted member of this group. Kanga and her son Roo, characters in A. A. Milne’s stories about Winnie-the-Pooh, are also members of this group.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this group of mammals whose babies, called joeys, usually grow in a pouch.

tossups.p: The honey possum, a mouse-sized member of this group, is one of the few mammals that feed only on nectar and pollen, which it laps up with a long, brush-tipped tongue. The possums of Australia and the opossums of the Americas are different animals, but both belong to this group.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this group of mammals, including kangaroos and koalas, that usually raise their young in a pouch.

tossups.p: Members of this group have a pair of epipubic [“ep-ih-PYOO-bik”] bones that jut forward from the hips, a feature they share with the egg-laying monotremes. Unlike monotremes, members of this group give birth to live young after a very short pregnancy, often lasting only a few weeks.
tossups.r: Their tiny newborns crawl into a pouch. For 10 points, name this group of mammals.

tossups.p: Many members of this group can put an early embryo on hold for months, a process called embryonic diapause [“DY-uh-pawz”], so that a new baby develops only when the timing is right. The newborn of the largest living member of this group is only about the size of a jellybean.
tossups.r: Those newborns crawl into the mother’s pouch on their own. For 10 points, name this group of mammals, including kangaroos.

trap.title: Pouches versus eggs
trap.body: Australia is also home to the platypus and the echidnas, which are monotremes: mammals that lay eggs instead of giving birth to tiny young. Some look-alikes and sound-alikes are actually placental mammals, such as kangaroo rats (rodents) and flying squirrels, and the koala “bear” is not a bear at all. Answering a single animal, like “kangaroos,” loses a tossup that asks for the whole group.
trap.fix: Pouches, joeys, opossums, epipubic bones, or tiny newborns that crawl to the pouch mean marsupials. Eggs, the platypus, or echidnas mean monotremes, and a long pregnancy fed by a long-lasting placenta means placental mammals. If the question says “this group” or “these mammals,” give the group name.
trap.line: Real answer line: Marsupials (accept Marsupialia, metatherians, or pouched mammals; prompt on mammals; do not accept “monotremes” or “placental mammals”)
